subject: surgery
title: Flap Classification, Local Transposition, and Free Tissue Transfer

steps.tx: In reconstructive plastic surgery, distinguishing between a graft and a flap is fundamental to wound reconstruction. While a skin graft relies completely upon recipient bed capillary **inosculation** for its survival, a flap carries its own intact or surgically restored blood supply. Flaps represent the reconstructive modality of choice when covering avascular wound beds such as bare cortical bone devoid of periosteum, exposed tendons lacking paratenon, joint cavities, or synthetic prosthetic hardware where free skin grafts invariably fail.
steps.say: Unlike a skin graft that requires nutrient uptake and capillary inosculation from the recipient bed, a flap carries its own dedicated blood supply. Flaps can successfully cover bare bone, exposed tendons, and irradiated defects.

left.title: Skin Graft
points: Lacks intrinsic vascular blood supply
Requires vascularised granulating recipient bed
Survives via imbibition and inosculation
Cannot cover bare bone or tendon

right.title: Surgical Flap
points: Maintains intact intrinsic vascular pedicle
Provides own blood flow and lymphatic drainage
Brings independent tissue vascularity
Successfully covers avascular structures

steps.tx: Flaps are classified according to their intrinsic vascular architecture into random pattern and axial pattern varieties. A **random pattern flap** lacks a named anatomically identifiable vascular axis, relying instead on microvascular perfusion delivered through the subdermal and dermal capillary plexuses. Consequently, random flaps possess strict geometrical constraints and generally require a length-to-width ratio not exceeding two to one on the trunk and extremities, though highly vascular facial tissues safely permit a three to one ratio.
steps.say: Random pattern flaps rely on the unoriented subdermal plexus rather than a single named artery. They are restricted to strict length-to-width ratios to prevent distal ischaemic necrosis.

rows: Small local facial defects; simple wound closures
No strict ratio; length determined by angiosome
Groin flap; deltopectoral flap; forehead flap
Extensive paddle based on single perforator

steps.tx: Reconstruction of small to moderate adjacent cutaneous defects relies predominantly on versatile **local flaps**, which are harvested immediately contiguous with the surgical wound. Local flaps are categorized into advancement, pivotal, and interpolation designs. Advancement flaps glide directly forward into the defect along a straight linear vector without rotational distortion, exemplified by simple single-pedicle advancement or V-Y advancement flaps. In a V-Y closure, a triangular island flap is advanced forward into the defect, and the donor gap is closed in a straight line.
steps.say: Local flaps are recruited immediately adjacent to a wound defect. Advancement flaps move straight forward into the wound, whereas pivotal flaps rotate around an anatomical anchor point.

nodes.label: Evaluate Tissue Laxity and Langer Lines
Mobilise Flap and Close Primary and Secondary Defects

steps.tx: Pivotal flaps rotate around a fixed pivot point and encompass rotation flaps and transposition flaps. A classic **transposition flap**, such as the Limberg rhomboid flap or Webster bilobed flap, is lifted over an intervening bridge of intact normal skin and transposed into an adjacent defect. Geometric planning must account for the inevitable functional shortening of the flap radius as it rotates through its arc. The resulting secondary donor site is either sutured primarily or covered with a split-thickness skin graft.
steps.say: Transposition flaps like the Limberg rhomboid flap move laterally across intact skin to fill a neighbouring defect. Surgeons must account for radial shortening as the flap rotates through its arc.

steps.tx: When reconstructing larger composite tissue defects, surgeons utilize robust regional **pedicled flaps** transferred from an anatomical site separated from the wound. These axial flaps remain connected to their donor origin by a vascular leash containing a recognized artery and vein. Prominent examples include the deltopectoral flap based on the internal mammary perforators, the pectoralis major myocutaneous flap supplied by the pectoral branch of the thoracoacromial axis, and the latissimus dorsi flap nourished by the thoracodorsal neurovascular bundle.
steps.say: Pedicled flaps are harvested from distant regions while remaining tethered to their primary vascular pedicle. The pectoralis major and latissimus dorsi flaps provide excellent bulk and reliable perfusion.

rows: Head and neck mucosal and cutaneous reconstruction
Latissimus muscle with or without skin paddle
Autologous breast reconstruction; thoracic wall defects
Pharyngeal reconstruction; lower facial soft tissue loss
Axial forehead skin and frontalis muscle
Nasal reconstruction; nasal tip and ala replacement

steps.tx: Complex composite reconstruction of extensive oncological or traumatic defects has been revolutionized by microvascular **free flap** transfer. In this advanced procedure, a block of skin, muscle, bone, or intestine is completely detached from its donor site along with its dominant feeding artery and draining vein. The isolated tissue paddle is transferred to the recipient defect, where its pedicle vessels undergo microscopic end-to-end or end-to-side anastomoses to local recipient arteries and veins under operating microscope visualization.
steps.say: A free flap is completely detached from its donor site and reconnected to recipient vessels using microvascular anastomoses. This technique allows single-stage reconstruction of extensive complex defects.

left.title: Pedicled Flap
points: Remains attached to native vascular origin
Limited reach dictated by pedicle length
No microvascular anastomosis required
Technically simpler and faster

right.title: Microvascular Free Flap
points: Completely divided from native blood supply
Unlimited anatomical transfer reach
Requires operative microvascular surgery
Enables precise composite tissue tailoring

steps.tx: Selecting an optimal free flap depends on the precise structural tissue requirements of the recipient defect. When reconstructing full-thickness segmental mandibular defects following radical oral cancer resection, the osteocutaneous **fibula free flap** based on the peroneal vessels represents the undisputed gold standard, providing up to twenty-five centimetres of dense cortical bone suitable for osseointegrated dental implants. For thin, pliable soft tissue resurfacing of the tongue or floor of mouth, surgeons choose the radial forearm fasciocutaneous free flap.
steps.say: Free flap choice matches the missing tissue. The free fibula flap provides structural vascularized bone for mandibular reconstruction, while the radial forearm flap supplies pliable skin for oral lining.

Thin, pliable, hairless skin and fascia
Tongue, floor of mouth, and pharyngeal defects

steps.tx: The postoperative survival of a microvascular free flap hinges upon vigilant clinical and instrumented perfusion monitoring during the critical initial forty-eight to seventy-two hours. Thrombosis of the venous anastomosis is significantly more common and insidious than arterial occlusive failure. A failing flap with acute **venous thrombosis** becomes rapidly cyanotic, tensely swollen, and cool, exhibiting brisk dark bleeding upon pinprick testing. Immediate operative re-exploration, anastomotic revision, and mechanical thrombectomy within hours can successfully salvage the compromised flap.
steps.say: Free flap monitoring is critical because early venous thrombosis can destroy the reconstruction. A cyanotic, tense flap bleeding dark blood on pinprick mandates immediate emergency surgical re-exploration.

left.title: Arterial Occlusion
points: Flap becomes pale, marble-white, and cold
Capillary refill completely absent
Loss of Doppler arterial acoustic signals
No bleeding upon diagnostic skin needle pinprick

right.title: Venous Thrombosis
points: Flap becomes congested, cyanotic, and tense
Capillary refill becomes sluggish or falsely brisk
